meta.project: Pass It On - NASA Space Apps 2026, Abandoned but not Forgotten
meta.note: Facts come from NSSDCA and NASA Science pages listed in each entry's sources. Story, simple and chip text are our own wording based on those facts. Items marked verify:true were not on the pages read - check before shipping.
meta.dates: Dates are UTC as given by NSSDCA. NASA Science sometimes gives US dates (e.g. Spirit landed Jan 3, 2004 US time = Jan 4 UTC).
meta.coordinates: Moon coordinates are from NSSDCA (LRO-derived). Mars coordinates are landing sites as given by NSSDCA; longitudes in degrees east.

images.selection: Photos were taken from the same NSSDCA and NASA Science pages as the facts, and each was viewed before being added. Photos where an astronaut is the main subject were left out.
images.uses: hero = main photo for the stop; fact-card = small photo on the card; scene = shown during a story line or answer (anim links it to an animation); background = wide panorama; drawing-reference = for the artist, not shown to kids as a photo of the real thing on the Moon or Mars.
images.hosting: Download these into the app (e.g. public/images/) instead of linking to NASA's servers, so the demo works on slow Wi-Fi and if pages move.
images.credit: Show the credit line under each photo, and list NSSDCA and NASA Science in the submission's data references. Don't use the NASA logo.

machines.name: Surveyor 3

facts.site: Southeastern Oceanus Procellarum (Ocean of Storms), inside a 200 m crater on a 14 degree slope
facts.landingStory: Its radar was confused by bright rocks and its engines kept firing, so it touched down three times before settling.
facts.work: Took 6,326 TV pictures and dug trenches up to 18 cm deep with its scoop.
facts.discovery: Lunar soil was like wet sand and strong enough to hold an Apollo lunar module.
facts.howItEnded: It did not wake up after the two-week lunar night.
facts.afterlife: On 1969-11-20 Apollo 12 astronauts Pete Conrad and Alan Bean walked over and removed about 10 kg of parts, including the TV camera, to study back on Earth. The camera is now at the Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: Hello, rookie! I'm Surveyor 3, a robot lander. I've been sitting in a small crater on the Moon since April 1967.
story.simple: Hi! I'm Surveyor 3, a robot that landed on the Moon in 1967. I'm still sitting there today.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: Back then, nobody knew what the Moon's ground was really like. Was it hard rock, or deep, soft dust that a spaceship might sink into?
story.simple: Nobody knew if the Moon's ground was hard or soft. A spaceship might sink into soft dust!

story.speaker: quill
story.text: So NASA sent you first, before any astronauts?
story.simple: So you went first, before any people?

story.speaker: machine
story.text: Exactly! My job was to land gently, test the ground, and tell NASA whether it was safe to send people.
story.simple: Yes! I had to land gently, test the ground, and tell NASA if people could land safely.
story.onScreen: Job: test the ground for astronauts

story.speaker: machine
story.text: Engineers at the Hughes Aircraft Company built me, for NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory. The whole Surveyor programme cost 469 million dollars.
story.simple: A company called Hughes Aircraft built me. All of the Surveyor robots together cost 469 million dollars.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: On 17 April 1967 an Atlas-Centaur rocket launched me. Three days later, on 20 April, I reached the Moon.
story.simple: A big rocket launched me. Three days later I got to the Moon.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: My landing was bumpy. Bright rocks confused my radar, my engines kept firing, and I touched down three times before I finally settled.
story.simple: My landing went wrong in a funny way. I bounced off the ground twice before I finally stopped.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: This is a Surveyor just like me, photographed on Earth. I'm about 3 meters tall and weigh 296 kilograms. My landing legs have round footpads that spread my weight on the ground.
story.simple: This is a robot just like me, photographed on Earth. I'm almost twice as tall as a grown-up, with legs and round feet.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: My TV camera took the pictures, my antenna sent them home by radio, and my solar panel turned sunlight into electricity to power everything.
story.simple: I had a camera to take pictures, an antenna to send them home, and a solar panel that made electricity from sunlight.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: I also had a scoop on an arm. Scientists on Earth sent me commands, and I dug little trenches up to 18 centimeters deep and pressed on the soil to see how strong it was.
story.simple: I had a little shovel on an arm. I dug small holes in the dirt and pushed on it to see how firm it was.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: Altogether, my camera sent home 6,326 pictures of the Moon around me.
story.simple: I took lots and lots of photos. More than six thousand!

story.speaker: machine
story.text: Here's what I found: the Moon's soil felt like wet sand, and it was strong enough to hold up an Apollo lunar module. That told NASA that astronauts could land.
story.simple: The Moon's dirt was firm, like wet sand at the beach. So a spaceship with people wouldn't sink.
story.onScreen: Soil like wet sand: safe to land

story.speaker: quill
story.text: Why didn't you fly back home afterwards?
story.simple: Why didn't you come home?

story.speaker: machine
story.text: I was built for a one-way trip. When the two-week lunar night came, it got dark and very cold. I fell asleep on 4 May 1967 and never woke up.
story.simple: I was only ever going one way. When the long, dark, cold night came, my power ran out and I went to sleep for good.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: But I wasn't forgotten. In November 1969, Apollo 12 astronauts Pete Conrad and Alan Bean landed nearby, walked over, and took my camera home. It's in a museum in Washington, D.C. today.
story.simple: Later, two astronauts landed near me and came to visit! They took my camera back to Earth, and now it's in a museum.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: Studying my parts showed engineers how materials change after two and a half years on the Moon. That matters for Artemis, because new missions need equipment that lasts on the Moon for a long time.
story.simple: Scientists studied my old parts to learn how things change on the Moon. That helps them build better machines for new Moon trips.

chips.a: I was built for a one-way trip. My job was to test the ground for the astronauts, not to fly home.
No. I stopped talking to Earth on May 4, 1967, after the Sun set. I've been resting in my crater ever since.
Apollo 12 astronauts took it home in 1969. Now it's in a museum in Washington, D.C., so people can see a camera that lived on the Moon.

lesson.text: Test the ground before you send people, and study how machines age in space.
lesson.nextMission: Artemis missions need equipment that can survive on the Moon for a long time.

machines.backOnEarth: The parts Apollo 12 brought home let engineers study how materials change after two and a half years on the Moon.

machines.name: Apollo 12 ALSEP (Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package)

facts.site: Oceanus Procellarum, about 180 m from Surveyor 3
facts.power: SNAP-27 radioisotope thermoelectric generator (RTG), about 70 W, heated by a plutonium-238 fuel capsule
facts.firstMoonquakeMadeByPeople: After the astronauts left, the empty lunar module ascent stage was crashed into the Moon about 60 km away, creating the first recorded artificial moonquake for the seismometer.
facts.howItEnded: Switched off from Earth on 30 September 1977, along with all the other ALSEP stations.
facts.descentStage: The descent stage of the lunar module Intrepid served as the launch platform for the ascent stage and was left behind on the Moon.
facts.apollo11Eagle: Apollo 11's lunar module Eagle also left its descent stage on the Moon in July 1969, as a launch platform.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: Hi there! I'm the science station that Apollo 12 left on the Moon in November 1969. My job was to keep doing science after the astronauts went home.
story.simple: Hi! I'm a set of science tools that astronauts left on the Moon. I kept working after they went home.

story.speaker: quill
story.text: Why leave science behind? Couldn't the astronauts just do the experiments themselves?
story.simple: Why leave tools behind? Couldn't the astronauts do the science?

story.speaker: machine
story.text: Astronauts could only stay on the Moon for a day or two. Some questions take years to answer, like how often the Moon shakes. So NASA left me to keep measuring.
story.simple: Astronauts could only stay a short time. Some science takes years, so I stayed to keep watching.
story.onScreen: Science that keeps going for years

story.speaker: machine
story.text: The Bendix Corporation in Ann Arbor, Michigan, designed and built science stations like me. When NASA chose Bendix in 1966, it expected the first four stations to cost about 17 million dollars.
story.simple: A company called Bendix in Michigan built me. The first four science stations were expected to cost about 17 million dollars.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: I launched on 14 November 1969 on a giant Saturn V rocket, packed inside the Apollo 12 lunar module, Intrepid. Five days later, on 19 November, we landed.
story.simple: I rode to the Moon packed inside the astronauts' spaceship, on a giant rocket.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: We landed in the Ocean of Storms, only about 180 meters from Surveyor 3. Astronauts Pete Conrad and Alan Bean carried me out and set me up by hand.
story.simple: We landed right next to Surveyor 3! Two astronauts carried me out and set me up.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: Let me show you my parts. My central station was my brain and my radio. Flat cables connected it to my instruments, and its antenna sent their measurements to Earth, day and night.
story.simple: My middle box was like my brain. It collected what my tools measured and sent it home by radio.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: I had no solar panels. Instead, a generator heated by plutonium-238 turned heat into about 70 watts of electricity, day and night. That's roughly enough for one bright light bulb.
story.simple: Instead of sunlight, I used a special heater that turns heat into electricity. It worked even in the dark.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: My most important instrument was a seismometer. It's like a super-sensitive ear pressed to the ground, feeling for the tiniest shakes.
story.simple: My best tool could feel the Moon shake, even a tiny bit.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: I also measured the Moon's magnetism, the stream of tiny particles that blows from the Sun, called the solar wind, Moon dust, and the Moon's very thin layer of gas.
story.simple: I also measured magnets, the wind of tiny bits from the Sun, dust, and the Moon's very thin gas.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: Then something clever happened. After the astronauts left, the empty top part of their lunar module was crashed into the Moon on purpose, about 60 kilometers away.
story.simple: After the astronauts left, scientists crashed an empty part of their spaceship into the Moon on purpose.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: I felt the crash! It was the first moonquake ever made by people. Scientists studied how the shaking travelled through the Moon, a bit like tapping a melon to check what's inside.
story.simple: I felt the Moon wobble, like a drum after you hit it. That told scientists about the inside of the Moon.

story.speaker: quill
story.text: What did all that shaking teach scientists?
story.simple: What did the shaking teach them?

story.speaker: machine
story.text: How shaking travels depends on what it passes through. So my measurements helped scientists learn what the inside of the Moon is like, and that helps us understand how rocky worlds like Earth are built.
story.simple: The way shaking moves tells scientists what's deep inside the Moon. That helps them understand Earth too.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: Something else stayed here with me: the bottom half of the lunar module. The astronauts used it as their launch pad to blast off, then left it behind. Apollo 11's Eagle left one too.
story.simple: The bottom of the astronauts' spaceship stayed here too. It was their launch pad for going home.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: I sent data home for almost eight years. On 30 September 1977, NASA switched me off from Earth, along with all the other Apollo science stations.
story.simple: I worked for almost eight years. Then NASA turned me off from Earth.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: Now new science instruments are planned for the Artemis landing sites, to carry on what I started.
story.simple: Soon, new science tools will go to the Moon with Artemis.

chips.a: That was the plan! Astronauts could only stay a day or two, so they left me to keep doing science for years after they went home.
No. NASA switched off all the Apollo science stations on 30 September 1977.
Surveyor 3! Apollo 12 landed about 180 meters away from it, and the astronauts walked over to visit.

chips.q: What else did Apollo 12 leave here?
chips.a: The bottom half of the lunar module, Intrepid. The astronauts used it as a launch pad to take off, and it stayed behind on the Moon. Apollo 11's Eagle left its bottom half too, back in July 1969.

lesson.text: Leave science behind that keeps working after people go home.
lesson.nextMission: New science instruments planned for Artemis landing sites.

machines.backOnEarth: Studying moonquakes helps scientists understand how rocky worlds, including Earth, are built inside.

machines.name: Lunar Roving Vehicle (Apollo 15)

facts.site: Hadley-Apennine, Mare Imbrium, at the foot of the Apennine mountains
facts.siteNote: Coordinates are the Apollo 15 lunar module landing site; the rover was left near it.
facts.wheels: Woven zinc-coated steel wire tires with titanium chevrons for grip; each wheel had its own electric motor
facts.navigation: A gyro and odometer fed a computer that tracked the way back to the lunar module; a Sun-shadow device gave a backup heading
facts.foldUp: Folded up to fit in a bay on the side of the lunar module
facts.firstUse: Apollo 15 was the first time a rover like this was used on the Moon.
facts.otherRovers: Three LRVs were driven on the Moon: Apollo 15, 16 and 17. Apollo 17's went 35.9 km.
facts.alsoAtSite: Apollo 15 ALSEP science station (seven instruments, including a heat flow experiment), switched off 1977-09-30
facts.howItEnded: Parked on the Moon when the astronauts left on 1971-08-02. Its batteries were never meant to be recharged.
facts.descentStage: The descent stage of the lunar module Falcon served as the launch platform for the ascent stage and was left behind on the Moon.
facts.laserReflector: Apollo 15 left a laser ranging retroreflector with 300 corner-cube mirrors; the Apollo 11 and 14 arrays have 100 each. Observatories on Earth still fire lasers at these reflectors to measure the Earth-Moon distance.
facts.topSpeed: On level ground the Apollo 15 rover reached a maximum of about 13 km/h (7 mph). The Apollo 16 rover later reached 17 km/h going downhill.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: Hop in! I'm the Lunar Roving Vehicle from Apollo 15, the moon buggy. I've been parked at the foot of the Moon's Apennine mountains since 1971.
story.simple: Hi! I'm a car for the Moon, a moon buggy. I've been parked on the Moon since 1971.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: Walking on the Moon in a big spacesuit is slow, hard work, so astronauts couldn't go far from their lander. NASA built me so they could drive much farther and explore more places.
story.simple: Walking in a spacesuit is hard work. I let astronauts drive much farther.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: The Boeing company built me, with a company called Delco as a big helper. The contract started at 19 million dollars, but the rovers ended up costing 38 million.
story.simple: A company called Boeing built me. I cost 38 million dollars, twice what was planned.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: On 26 July 1971 I launched with Apollo 15, folded up flat in a bay on the side of the lunar module, Falcon. Four days later we landed at Hadley.
story.simple: I traveled to the Moon folded up small, like a camping chair, on the side of the spaceship.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: Once we landed, the astronauts unfolded me from the side of the lander, and I was ready to drive.
story.simple: On the Moon, the astronauts unfolded me and I was ready to go.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: Let me show you my parts. I'm electric, and each of my four wheels has its own motor. My tires are woven from zinc-coated steel wire, with titanium strips for grip, instead of air-filled rubber.
story.simple: I run on batteries, like a toy car. Each wheel has its own motor, and my tires are made of metal mesh instead of rubber.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: My power came from two 36-volt silver-zinc batteries. They couldn't be recharged, so every drive was planned carefully.
story.simple: I had two big batteries. They couldn't be charged again, so the astronauts planned their drives carefully.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: I'm 3.1 meters long and weigh 210 kilograms, but I could carry 490 kilograms: two astronauts in spacesuits plus their tools and rock samples. They drove me with a hand controller.
story.simple: I'm longer than a sofa, and I could carry two astronauts plus their tools and rocks.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: There's no GPS on the Moon. A gyro and an odometer fed a small computer that always knew the way back to the lander, and a little Sun-shadow tool worked as a backup compass.
story.simple: There are no road signs on the Moon! My tools remembered how far and which way we went, so we never got lost.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: Astronauts David Scott and James Irwin drove me 27.8 kilometers, in 3 hours and 2 minutes of driving. Our longest trip was 12.5 kilometers, and we went as far as 5 kilometers from the lander.
story.simple: Two astronauts drove me a long way, much farther than they could walk.

story.speaker: quill
story.text: Were you the only moon buggy?
story.simple: Are you the only moon buggy?

story.speaker: machine
story.text: No! Apollo 15 was the first time a rover like me was used on the Moon. Two more followed on Apollo 16 and 17, and Apollo 17's drove 35.9 kilometers. All three are still parked on the Moon.
story.simple: There are three moon buggies on the Moon. I was the first one.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: Not everything here is asleep. The astronauts also set up a laser reflector with 300 small mirrors, and scientists on Earth still bounce laser beams off it to measure how far away the Moon is.
story.simple: Something near me still works! It's a panel of mirrors. Scientists shine a laser at it from Earth and time how long the light takes to come back.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: When the astronauts left on 2 August 1971, I stayed parked here for good. I was built for a one-way trip, and my batteries couldn't be recharged.
story.simple: When the astronauts flew home, I stayed parked on the Moon. I was built for a one-way trip.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: The bottom half of Falcon stayed here with me. It was the launch pad the astronauts blasted off from.
story.simple: The bottom of their spaceship stayed too. It was their launch pad.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: Artemis astronauts will drive a new lunar rover too, so they can explore far, just like we did.
story.simple: Soon Artemis astronauts will drive a new Moon car, just like me.

chips.a: I was built for a one-way trip, and my batteries couldn't be recharged, so I was always going to stay on the Moon.
On flat ground I reached about 13 kilometers per hour, a bit faster than you can jog. A later moon buggy on Apollo 16 hit 17 kilometers per hour going downhill!
Yes! Three were driven on the Moon, on Apollo 15, 16 and 17. Apollo 17's buggy drove 35.9 km.
Yes! The laser reflector Apollo 15 left near me has 300 little mirrors. Scientists on Earth still bounce lasers off it to measure exactly how far away the Moon is.
The bottom half of the lunar module Falcon, which was the astronauts' launch pad, the Apollo 15 science station, and the laser reflector.

lesson.text: Wheels let explorers go much farther and do more science.
lesson.nextMission: Artemis astronauts will also drive a new lunar rover.

machines.backOnEarth: Driving lets explorers bring back rocks from many places, not just next to the lander.

machines.name: Viking 1 and Viking 2 Landers

viking1.endNote: NASA Science: stopped operating 11 Nov 1982 after a faulty command. NSSDCA: contact lost 13 Nov 1982.

viking2.site: Utopia Planitia, about 200 km west of crater Mie
viking2.landingQuirk: Settled with one leg on a rock, tilted 8.2 degrees
viking2.endNote: Turned off when its batteries failed, after 1,281 Mars days.

facts.power: Two radioisotope thermoelectric generators (plutonium-238) per lander
facts.firsts: Viking 1 made NASA's first truly successful landing on Mars and sent the first images from the surface.
facts.photos: The two landers returned 4,500 photos of their landing sites.
facts.cleanliness: Each lander was sealed in a bioshield at launch so Earth germs wouldn't reach Mars.
facts.lifeSearch: Their main goal was to look for evidence of life on Mars.
facts.lifeResult: Data from the soil samples could be read as a weak positive for life, but the main test for organic compounds gave negative results. Scientists still debate the results, and the question of life on Mars remains open.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: We're the Viking landers, a pair of twins! Viking 1 made NASA's first truly successful landing on Mars in July 1976, and Viking 2 joined in September.
story.simple: We're two robot twins. One of us was the first NASA robot to land safely on Mars.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: We were sent to help answer one of the biggest questions ever: is there life on Mars?
story.simple: We went to find out if anything lives on Mars.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: A company called Martin Marietta built us landers, working for NASA's Langley Research Center. The whole Viking mission, two landers plus two spacecraft that circled Mars, cost roughly one billion dollars.
story.simple: A company called Martin Marietta built us. Our whole mission cost roughly a billion dollars.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: Viking 1 launched on 20 August 1975 and landed on 20 July 1976. Viking 2 launched on 9 September 1975 and landed on 3 September 1976.
story.simple: It took us almost a year to get to Mars and land.

story.speaker: quill
story.text: Wait! If you're looking for life, what if you carried Earth germs by mistake?
story.simple: But what if you carried germs from Earth?

story.speaker: machine
story.text: Good thinking! Before launch, each of us was sealed inside a bioshield, so Earth germs couldn't reach Mars and confuse our tests.
story.simple: We were sealed in a special cover before launch, so no Earth germs came along.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: Here's a drawing of one of us. Each lander weighs 572 kilograms and stands on landing legs. Two generators heated by plutonium-238 gave each of us power, so we didn't need sunshine.
story.simple: This is a drawing of us. We had legs and special heater-generators for power.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: We each had two cameras, a weather station on a little boom, a seismometer to feel for marsquakes, and a sampler arm to scoop up soil.
story.simple: We had two cameras, a weather station, and an arm with a scoop.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: Inside, we carried a tiny biology lab to test soil for signs of life, an instrument that searched the soil for carbon-based chemicals, and one that found out what the soil was made of.
story.simple: Inside us was a tiny lab to test the dirt for life.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: Seconds after landing, Viking 1 started sending the first picture ever taken on the surface of Mars. It arrived line by line, and you can see one of its own footpads!
story.simple: Right after landing, Viking 1 took the very first photo on Mars. It showed its own foot!
story.onScreen: First photo from the surface of Mars

story.speaker: machine
story.text: We scooped up soil with our arms, fed it into our labs, measured the weather, and together sent home 4,500 photos of our landing sites.
story.simple: We scooped dirt, tested it, checked the weather and took thousands of photos.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: So, did we find life? One test gave a weak sign that might have been life. But another test found no carbon-based chemicals in the soil. Scientists still argue about it, so the big question is still open.
story.simple: Did we find life? One test said maybe, another said no. Scientists still aren't sure.

story.speaker: quill
story.text: Why didn't you come back to Earth?
story.simple: Why didn't you come home?

story.speaker: machine
story.text: Leaving Mars would need a big rocket, and we were built to stay and do science where we landed. Viking 2 worked until its batteries failed in April 1980, after 1,281 Mars days. Viking 1 kept going until November 1982.
story.simple: We were built to stay. Viking 2 worked for almost four years, and Viking 1 for more than six.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: Today Viking 1 stands in Chryse Planitia and Viking 2 in Utopia Planitia, about 6,460 kilometers apart. Each of us is now named after a scientist from our team.
story.simple: We're still standing where we landed, far apart on Mars.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: Rovers that came after us, like Perseverance, keep asking our question: was Mars ever a place where life could live?
story.simple: Rovers since then, like Perseverance, keep asking: could Mars ever have had life?

chips.a: One of our tests gave a weak sign that might have been life. But another test found no carbon-based chemicals in the soil. Scientists still argue about it, so the big question is still open.
Getting off Mars needs a big rocket. We were built to stay and do science where we landed.
Viking 1 is in Chryse Planitia and Viking 2 is in Utopia Planitia, about 6,460 km apart. We're both still standing where we landed.

lesson.text: Land safely, keep things clean, and ask the big question: was Mars ever home to life?
lesson.nextMission: Later rovers, like Perseverance, keep asking whether Mars was once a place where life could live.

machines.backOnEarth: Comparing Mars' weather and soil with Earth's helps scientists understand how planets change.

facts.power: 0.2 square meters of solar cells, with backup batteries
facts.computer: Intel 80C85 8-bit processor, about 100,000 instructions per second
facts.signalDelay: 10 to 15 minutes each way, so it needed its own hazard avoidance
facts.landing: Airbags inflated around the lander; it hit the ground at 18 m/s, bounced about 12 m high and at least 15 more times, rolling to a stop about 2.5 minutes later and 1 km away.
facts.returned: More than 16,500 images from the lander and 550 from the rover, plus more than 15 chemical analyses of rocks and soil
facts.finding: Results suggest Mars was once warm and wet.
facts.howItEnded: Communications were lost for unknown reasons on 27 September 1997. The rover talked to Earth only through the lander.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: Hi! I'm Sojourner, the very first rover to drive on Mars. I weigh just 10.5 kilograms, about as much as a small dog.
story.simple: I'm the very first robot car on Mars. I'm tiny, about the size of a microwave oven.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: I was a test. NASA wanted to prove that a small, low-cost rover could land on Mars and drive around.
story.simple: I was a test, to show that a small robot car could work on Mars.
story.onScreen: Job: prove a small rover can work

story.speaker: machine
story.text: Engineers at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California built me. Developing me cost about 25 million dollars, which is very little for a Mars mission.
story.simple: Engineers in California built me. I cost about 25 million dollars, which is cheap for a Mars robot.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: A Delta II rocket launched me on 4 December 1996. I rode to Mars tucked onto my lander, and we arrived on 4 July 1997.
story.simple: A rocket launched me, and seven months later I reached Mars.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: Our landing was wild! Giant airbags puffed up around my lander. We hit the ground at 18 meters per second, bounced about 12 meters high, then bounced at least 15 more times.
story.simple: We landed inside giant balloons and bounced like a beach ball, higher than a house!

story.speaker: machine
story.text: About two and a half minutes later, we rolled to a stop about 1 kilometer away. Then the airbags deflated, and my lander opened up like a flower.
story.simple: After lots of bouncing we rolled to a stop, and my lander opened up like a flower.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: Two days later, on 6 July 1997, I rolled down a ramp onto Mars.
story.simple: Two days later, I drove down a ramp onto Mars.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: I'm only 63 centimeters long and 28 centimeters high, about the size of a microwave oven. My six wheels sit on a rocker-bogie suspension, which lets them climb over rocks while I stay steady.
story.simple: I'm about as big as a microwave oven, with six wheels that climb over rocks.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: On my back is a solar panel, just 0.2 square meters of solar cells, with backup batteries. My brain was a tiny computer that did about 100,000 instructions a second, much slower than a phone today.
story.simple: A solar panel on my back made my power, and I had a tiny computer brain.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: I couldn't talk to Earth by myself. I sent my pictures and measurements to my lander, and the lander sent them home.
story.simple: I passed my messages to my lander, and it sent them to Earth.
story.onScreen: Talked to Earth through the lander

story.speaker: machine
story.text: Radio messages took 10 to 15 minutes to travel between Earth and Mars. If I waited for drivers on Earth to spot a rock, I'd already have bumped into it!
story.simple: Messages took a long time to reach Earth, so drivers couldn't steer me quickly.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: So I had my own hazard avoidance: I spotted obstacles and steered around them by myself.
story.simple: So I learned to spot rocks and drive around them by myself.

story.speaker: quill
story.text: But how could you tell what a rock was made of, just by driving up to it?
story.simple: How did you know what the rocks were made of?

story.speaker: machine
story.text: I drove up to rocks with funny nicknames, like Moe, and pressed my instrument against them to find out what they're made of. I did more than 15 chemical tests of rocks and soil.
story.simple: I drove up to rocks and touched them with a special tool to find out what they're made of.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: My lander and I sent home more than 16,500 pictures from the lander and 550 from me. Our results suggest that Mars was once warm and wet.
story.simple: We sent home thousands of pictures, and clues that Mars was once warm and wet.
story.onScreen: Mars was once warm and wet

story.speaker: machine
story.text: On 27 September 1997, my lander stopped talking to Earth, and nobody knows why. Because I could only talk through my lander, I went quiet too.
story.simple: One day my lander stopped talking to Earth, and so did I.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: Spirit and Opportunity came next. They landed with airbags and drove on rocker-bogie wheels, just like me.
story.simple: My bigger rover cousins came next, and they used airbags and wheels just like mine.

chips.a: I was a test. NASA wanted to prove a small, low-cost rover could land and drive on Mars. Coming home was never part of the plan.

chips.q: Why couldn't NASA just drive you?
chips.a: Messages took 10 to 15 minutes each way. If I waited for Earth to see a rock, I'd already have hit it, so I steered around hazards myself.
My bigger siblings, Spirit and Opportunity. They also landed using airbags, just like me.

lesson.text: Robots far from home must think for themselves, and airbags can make landing cheaper.
lesson.nextMission: Spirit and Opportunity used airbag landings and rocker-bogie wheels too.

machines.backOnEarth: Robots that steer themselves around obstacles are now a big part of technology on Earth too.

machines.name: Spirit and Opportunity (Mars Exploration Rovers)

spirit.site: Gusev Crater, which looks like an old lakebed
spirit.stuck: On 2009-04-23 it broke through a thin crust into sand; by 2009-05-01 it could no longer move.
spirit.howItEnded: Stuck in sand, it couldn't tilt its solar panels toward the Sun to survive the winter.

opportunity.site: Meridiani Planum (Terra Meridiani), the 'Hematite Site', inside a 20 m crater
opportunity.howItEnded: A planet-wide dust storm blanketed its solar panels in June 2018.
opportunity.recordHandoff: Its off-Earth driving record held until 2026-10-11, when NASA's Perseverance rover passed it at 45.22 km.

facts.wheels: Six wheels on a rocker-bogie suspension, each with its own motor
facts.keyScience: By studying the rock record, Spirit and Opportunity confirmed that water was long-standing on the surface of Mars in ancient times.
facts.hematite: Hematite is an iron-rich mineral that typically forms in water.
facts.designLife: The primary mission was 90 sols (Mars days).
facts.missionDeclaredOver: verify: Opportunity's mission was declared over in February 2019 - confirm date from a NASA source.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: We're Spirit and Opportunity, twin robot geologists. A geologist studies rocks to learn a planet's story.
story.simple: We're twin robot rock scientists. Rocks tell us the story of a planet.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: NASA sent us to read the rocks and soil of Mars for clues about water long ago.
story.simple: We went to look for clues that Mars once had water.
story.onScreen: Job: look for signs of water

story.speaker: machine
story.text: Engineers at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California built and tested us. Building, launching and landing both of us, then running us for our first 90 Mars days, cost 820 million dollars.
story.simple: Engineers in California built us. Both of us together cost 820 million dollars.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: Two Delta II rockets launched us separately in the summer of 2003. Spirit landed on 4 January 2004, and Opportunity three weeks later, on 25 January.
story.simple: Two rockets launched us, and about seven months later we landed on Mars.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: We landed on opposite sides of Mars, bouncing inside airbags like Sojourner. Spirit landed in Gusev Crater, which looks like an old lakebed. Opportunity rolled into a small crater at Meridiani Planum.
story.simple: We landed far apart, on opposite sides of Mars, bouncing in airbags.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: Each of us weighs 185 kilograms. We have six wheels on a rocker-bogie suspension, each with its own motor. Our top speed was only about 3.75 centimeters per second. Slow, but safe!
story.simple: We each have six wheels with their own motors. We drive slowly and carefully.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: Our cameras sit on a mast 1.4 meters tall, so we could look across the land in color and in 3D, like a person standing up to look around.
story.simple: Our cameras are up on a tall pole, so we can see far, like you standing on tiptoe.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: Our wing-shaped solar panels made electricity from sunlight. That worked well, until Mars dust covered them.
story.simple: Our solar wings made power from sunlight, until dust covered them.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: On our robotic arm we carried a microscope camera, two instruments that find out what rocks are made of, and a Rock Abrasion Tool.
story.simple: Our arm held a microscope and tools to study rocks.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: The Rock Abrasion Tool grinds away the dusty outside of a rock so we can see inside. The first rock Opportunity ground into, called McKittrick, got a hole about 4 millimeters deep.
story.simple: Our grinder scraped off the dusty outside of rocks so we could see inside.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: Opportunity spotted shiny little spheres in the rocks, and found a mineral called hematite. Hematite is rich in iron, and it usually forms in water.
story.simple: Opportunity found a mineral that usually forms in water. A big clue!

story.speaker: machine
story.text: By studying the rocks, we confirmed that water lasted on the surface of Mars a long time ago.
story.simple: The rocks showed us that long ago, Mars had water for a long time.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: We were planned to work for 90 Mars days. Spirit kept going for about six years, and Opportunity for more than fourteen!
story.simple: We were meant to work for three months. We kept going for years and years!

story.speaker: quill
story.text: So what happened to you both?
story.simple: What happened to you?

story.speaker: machine
story.text: In 2009 Spirit broke through a thin crust into soft sand and got stuck. It couldn't tilt its solar panels toward the Sun for the winter, and its last message came on 22 March 2010, after driving 7.73 kilometers.
story.simple: Spirit got stuck in soft sand, couldn't get enough sunlight, and went quiet in 2010.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: Opportunity drove 45.16 kilometers, a record for any vehicle beyond Earth. In June 2018 a planet-wide dust storm covered its solar panels, and its last message came on 10 June.
story.simple: Opportunity drove farther than any car on another world. Then a giant dust storm blocked the Sun, and it went quiet in 2018.

story.speaker: machine
story.text: Opportunity's record lasted until 11 October 2026, when the Perseverance rover passed it at 45.22 kilometers. Our journey continues through the rovers that came after us.
story.simple: This year a newer rover called Perseverance finally drove even farther. Our journey continues through new rovers!

chips.a: Flying back from Mars would need a whole rocket. We were built to explore as long as we could, then stay.
No. Spirit's last message was on 22 March 2010. Opportunity's was on 10 June 2018, during a huge dust storm.
NASA's Perseverance rover. On 11 October 2026 it passed 45.22 km, just beyond Opportunity's 45.16 km.

lesson.text: Solar power and soft sand are real dangers. Plan for dust storms and test the ground before you drive.
lesson.nextMission: Perseverance, which passed Opportunity's driving record in October 2026.

machines.backOnEarth: Finding where water once flowed on Mars helps scientists understand how a planet can change from wet to dry.
